HEADER
Date/Time: 2025-02-12 15:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Sara Lopez (Cobalt Lead ML Eng), Tom Nguyen (Cobalt Infra), Priya Rao (Cobalt Data Privacy)

AUTO-SUMMARY (auto-generated):
Short technical deep dive on JSON "structured output" (tool/function calling) performance. Discussed decoding overhead for JSON mode, constrained decoding strategies, KV cache interactions, batching tradeoffs, and quantization effects. Agreed next steps: Redwood to run benchmark harness on hosted and customer on-prem configs, customer to provide prompt sets and on-prem access, follow-up results review week of 2025-02-24.

TOPICS:
- JSON mode / tool-calling overhead
- Constrained decoding & structured output
- KV cache behavior with tool calls
- Batching and latency/throughput tradeoffs
- Quantization (int8/4) impact on decoding speed
- VPC/on-prem deployment considerations

TRANSCRIPT:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, i think we have about an hour, uh, want to kick off — this is a technical deep dive focused on JSON mode and tool-calling overhead, ravi's going to walk through perf tradeoffs, and we'll capture concrete benchmark asks.
[00:18] Sara: thanks maya, yeah from cobalt's side we care about stable 95th-percentile latency sub 300ms for single-call JSON outputs for our fraud detection hooks, and we have an on-prem requirement because of regulated data.
[00:35] Ravi: okay, high level for structured outputs there are two main sources of extra latency — one is token overhead for the model to serialise the JSON, and two is decoding complexity when you constrain generation (like schema-only tokens, forced keys, or sampled constrained decoding). these interact with batching and kv cache in non-obvious ways.
[01:02] Tom: can you explain kv cache impact? i thought caching prefixes would help a lot.
[01:10] Ravi: yes, kv cache helps when the request shares a prefix of tokens with previous requests — like the system prompt and few-shot examples. but for a tool call where the model emits structured json, the unique per-call arguments change suffix tokens so cache hits are lower. also many of our optimizations assume contiguous autoregressive decoding, but constrained decoding (like requiring a specific key order or exact brackets) causes more token-by-token checks which hurt batching.
[01:42] Sara: when you say checks do you mean like logit filtering and token masking?
[01:46] Ravi: exactly — mask vocab, set logit bias for keys, or use constrained beam to enforce schema. every time you apply a mask or a forced token list it adds CPU-side work per token and can break kernel fusion in the GPU runtime, so throughput drops and tail latency increases.
[02:10] Maya: is that why we see higher latencies for json mode vs freeform text in earlier benchmarks?
[02:15] Ravi: yes, json mode commonly shows 10–40% higher per-token cost in our measurements because of additional host-side logic and sometimes extra tokens for structural framing (like opening braces, quotes, commas). if you also stream partial json it's worse because you may not benefit from kv cache until the very end.
[02:38] Priya: from privacy side we need deterministic outputs and schema guarantees — we prefer constrained decoding to ensure no PII leaks in keys. but we also need predictable latencies.
[02:50] Ravi: that's the typical eat-your-veg tradeoff. you can reduce overhead by moving some enforcement server-side: accept model output and run a fast validator that repairs minor schema deviations. or do hybrid: enforce keys only but allow freeform values, or use a two-pass approach where first pass generates a concise serialized callref token that maps to a stored structured payload — lower tokenisation cost.
[03:20] Tom: curious about quantization — does int4/int8 slow down constrained decoding more than normal?
[03:26] Ravi: quantization mostly affects the raw matmul performance; on GPU int8 typically gives better throughput. but for constrained decoding the bottleneck often shifts to host CPU (masks/logit bias), so the relative benefit of quantization shrinks. on CPU or on lower-end GPUs, int4 can reduce memory and improve cache, but you need to measure end-to-end latency including pop-run overhead and any dequantization cost.
[03:55] Sara: what about batching — we rely on high qps for throughput; how does that interact with JSON mode?
[04:02] Ravi: batching helps when requests are similar and can be batched without increasing tail latency beyond SLOs. but constrained decoding and per-request schema enforcement often requires per-sample masks, which reduces batch kernel reuse. Also, if you need low p95 single-request latency you can't wait to build big batches. There's an optimization: adaptive batching where small latency-sensitive requests skip heavy constraints and go to a low-latency path, while bulk jobs use full constraints.
[04:38] Maya: could you sketch a recommended benchmark plan we can run on customer's on-prem cluster?
[04:44] Ravi: yes — we should measure these axes: 1) JSON unconstrained vs constrained (mask+logit bias) — measure p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec; 2) Quantization variants (fp16 vs int8 vs int4 if supported); 3) KV cache hit patterns (cold start, shared prefix, per-request unique); 4) Batch sizes (1, 4, 8, 16) under same load; 5) Streaming vs non-streaming generation; 6) Function-calling vs in-band json — function-calling adds framing tokens but can simplify parsing.
[05:20] Tom: ok we'll provide realistic prompt set and some long-ish examples. do you have a harness that supports on-prem runs and collects kernel-level metrics?
[05:28] Ravi: yes we have a benchmark harness (we'll share) that can run in the customer's env, collects per-token time, host-side mask latency, kernel occupancy, and end-to-end latency distributions. it also logs kv cache hit ratio. we'll need SSH or a secure agent to run it in their VPC — we can also provide Docker image.
[05:48] Sara: for tool-calling specifically — is the model's output always larger because of JSON syntax, or are there tricks to reduce token count?
[05:56] Ravi: both. JSON adds structural tokens; you can use compact encoding (no spaces, short keys), or use token aliasing: map frequently used keys to short tokens in a pre-shared schema. also use schema-driven prompts that ask the model to output a compressed call signature and then expand on server-side — tradeoff is extra server logic but fewer tokens.
[06:19] Priya: would streaming partial json expose PII earlier in the stream?
[06:24] Ravi: yes you might leak values earlier. For privacy-sensitive data, prefer non-streaming or enforce server-side redaction before streaming out. In on-prem, we can integrate KMS to ensure logs are encrypted and retention policies enforced.
[06:38] Maya: some customers asked about function-calling APIs where the model emits a function name and args — how is that different perf-wise?
[06:46] Ravi: function-calling is similar to structured JSON but often uses a canonical framing and a small set of field names, which can be optimized with fixed vocab bias — that reduces token uncertainty. However, if the arguments are large, token cost remains. Also, function calling may require extra parsing step which is cheap compared to constrained decoding, but overall latency is similar to a short JSON output.
[07:08] Sara: any kernel-level optimizations you plan to add on redwood side?
[07:12] Ravi: yes, we're working on tighter kernel fusion for masked decoding paths so logit filtering happens closer to the matmul result, reducing host-side work. also experimenting with precompiled constraint automata that run on GPU for common schemas — that would dramatically reduce CPU work per token.
[07:30] Tom: that sounds promising — timeline?
[07:33] Ravi: prototypes in 6–8 weeks, production-grade in a quarter depending on charters.
[07:40] Maya: let's talk about tradeoffs for on-prem: model size, GPU type, and quantization.
[07:45] Ravi: for on-prem the key is pick the smallest model that meets quality. smaller sequence length and token-efficiency reduces KV pressure. GPUs matter: A100 vs H100 have differences in int8/sparsity kernels. For inference-dominated workflows we recommend H100 when available; if not, A100 with int8 is reasonable. Also ensure PCIe bandwidth and host CPU isn't the bottleneck for constrained decoding.
[08:12] Sara: do you have concrete numbers for p95 per JSON output at ~150 tokens?
[08:17] Ravi: on our hosted profile with H100 and fp16, unconstrained 150-token output p95 ~180–220ms; constrained masks can push to 230–320ms depending on mask complexity. On int8 we see similar or slightly better raw matmul times but end-to-end only improves if host-side masking is addressed.
[08:42] Tom: if we do dedicated Redwood Dedicated would that change anything for us?
[08:46] Maya: Dedicated gives you reserved capacity and optimized kernels; we can tune kernel selection and batching behavior to your workload. For on-prem we can deploy our private runtime with similar tunings.
[08:59] Priya: compliance questions — do you log the raw outputs during benchmarks?
[09:04] Maya: we'll follow your retention and logging policies; for sensitive data we can run without storing outputs or with encrypted logs that you control.
[09:12] Ravi: one more note on batching & latency: we can expose a low-latency path that bypasses heavy constraints for requests that ask for it, and a high-accuracy path for batch processing. deciding which requests go where can be done with client-side flags or a routing policy.
[09:32] Sara: does constrained decoding always require beam search?
[09:36] Ravi: not necessarily; you can do constrained greedy decoding with masks. Beam gives higher success for complex constraints but at cost of multiple decoding rounds — more latency and tokens. For strict schema enforcement we often prefer constrained greedy plus a validator + repair pass.
[09:55] Tom: about streaming — you mentioned streaming hurts kv cache gains; can you clarify?
[10:00] Ravi: streaming commits to emitting tokens earlier, which means you can't batch later tokens; it reduces ability to aggregate token production across requests, lowering batching efficiency. Also early streaming prevents some cache reuse patterns because partial outputs differ more widely.
[10:20] Maya: ok let's move to concrete pilot ask — sara, tom, you'll share prompt set and expected schemas; we'll run these three scenarios on your on-prem cluster: a) unconstrained json full model, b) constrained masked json, c) hybrid compressed signature + server-expand. we'll collect p50/p95/p99, host-mask ms, kernel ms, kv-hit ratio.
[10:44] Sara: sounds good. timeline?
[10:46] Maya: we'll aim to run initial runs by 2025-02-19 and sync results the following week.
[10:52] Ravi: i'll include quantization runs too and a recommendation matrix for model/quant/instance types.
[10:58] Priya: please include data governance checklist — audit logs, KMS, SSO. we need that for our security review.
[11:05] Maya: noted. we'll attach our compliance pack.
[11:08] (brief cross-talk)
[11:18] Sara: one last question: if we need deterministic outputs, do you recommend sampling off?
[11:22] Ravi: yes set temperature to 0 and use greedy/constrained decoding; sampling increases non-determinism. deterministic plus validator/repair pipeline is common in regulated workloads.
[11:34] Tom: ok thanks everyone this was helpful.
[11:36] Maya: great, recap of next steps…
